# Discrete-event simulation {#sec-discrete-event-simulation}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own.
:::

@sec-jump-processes simulated the epidemic as a stream of events drawn from
population-level rates: the model knew how many susceptibles there were, not who
they were. This chapter keeps the event-driven view but moves it to the
individual, by writing down what a *person* does over time and letting a
scheduler interleave everybody's activities.

This is **discrete-event simulation**: the state changes only at events, time
jumps from one event to the next, and between events nothing happens. The style
is *process-oriented* — you write a function describing one individual's life
course, containing statements like "wait an exponentially distributed time, then
try to infect someone" — and the simulator maintains the event queue for you.

Two things follow that the earlier chapters cannot easily express. Waiting times
need not be exponential, because you simply draw from whatever distribution you
like before waiting, a theme taken up in @sec-non-exponential-periods. And
individuals can *contend for scarce resources* — hospital beds, ventilators,
test capacity — which is the natural language of queueing and has no counterpart
in a compartmental model.

## Learning goals

You will:

- distinguish process-oriented discrete-event simulation from the rate-based
  jump process of @sec-jump-processes;
- write an individual life course as a coroutine that waits and acts;
- run and record a `ConcurrentSim.jl` simulation of the SIR model;
- check it against the jump-process and ODE results; and
- recognise where discrete-event simulation earns its extra bookkeeping.

## Model assumptions and classification

The model is the baseline SIR process of @sec-jump-processes, expressed
individually: $N=1000$ people, of whom $I_0=10$ start infectious, contact rate
$c=10$, transmission probability $\beta=0.05$, recovery rate $\gamma=0.25$.

Each susceptible waits an $\operatorname{Exponential}(1/c)$ time until their next
contact, chooses a partner uniformly at random from the population, and becomes
infectious with probability $\beta$ if that partner is infectious. Each
infectious individual waits an $\operatorname{Exponential}(1/\gamma)$ time and
recovers.

This is a **stochastic, continuous-time, discrete-state, individual-level**
model, the same classification as the agent-based models of
@sec-agent-based-models. The difference is not what is represented but how time
advances: an agent-based model steps time forward in fixed increments and asks
every agent what it does, whereas here time jumps directly to the next scheduled
event and only the individual concerned acts.

## Equations

There are no differential equations to write. The model is defined by the two
waiting-time distributions and the contact rule:

$$
T_{\text{contact}} \sim \operatorname{Exponential}(1/c),
\qquad
T_{\text{recovery}} \sim \operatorname{Exponential}(1/\gamma).
$$ {#eq-ch08-waiting}

A contact transmits when the partner is infectious and an independent Bernoulli
draw succeeds with probability $\beta$. Because a susceptible contacts a uniformly
chosen individual, the chance that a given contact is with an infectious person
is $I/N$, so the population-level rate at which new infections occur is

$$
S \cdot c \cdot \beta \cdot \frac{I}{N} = \beta c\,\frac{SI}{N},
$$ {#eq-ch08-equivalence}

which is exactly the transmission propensity of @sec-jump-processes. The two
models describe the same process; only the bookkeeping differs. That equivalence
is what the Validation section tests.

## Julia implementation

`ConcurrentSim.jl` provides a `Simulation` holding the event queue, and
`@resumable` functions that may `@yield` a `timeout`. Yielding suspends the
process, returns control to the scheduler, and resumes it when the simulated
clock reaches that time. Each individual is one such process.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch08-setup
using ConcurrentSim
using ResumableFunctions
using Distributions
using Random
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using CairoMakie

const N = 1000
const I₀ = 10
const β = 0.05
const c = 10.0
const γ = 0.25
const tf = 40.0

mutable struct Person
    id::Int
    status::Symbol
end

mutable struct EpidemicModel
    sim::Simulation
    people::Vector{Person}
    times::Vector{Float64}
    susceptible::Vector{Int}
    infectious::Vector{Int}
    recovered::Vector{Int}
end

function record!(model::EpidemicModel)
    push!(model.times, now(model.sim))
    push!(model.susceptible, count(p -> p.status == :S, model.people))
    push!(model.infectious,  count(p -> p.status == :I, model.people))
    push!(model.recovered,   count(p -> p.status == :R, model.people))
    return nothing
end
```

The life course reads as prose: while still susceptible, wait for a contact and
possibly become infected; once infectious, wait once more and recover.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch08-process
@resumable function life_course(sim::Simulation, person::Person,
                                model::EpidemicModel, rng)
    while person.status == :S
        @yield timeout(sim, rand(rng, Exponential(1/c)))     # @eq-ch08-waiting
        partner = rand(rng, model.people)
        if partner.status == :I && rand(rng) < β
            person.status = :I
            record!(model)
        end
    end
    if person.status == :I
        @yield timeout(sim, rand(rng, Exponential(1/γ)))
        person.status = :R
        record!(model)
    end
end

function simulate_des(seed)
    sim = Simulation()
    people = [Person(i, i <= N - I₀ ? :S : :I) for i in 1:N]
    model = EpidemicModel(sim, people, [0.0], [N - I₀], [I₀], [0])
    rng = Xoshiro(seed)
    for person in people
        @process life_course(sim, person, model, rng)
    end
    run(sim, tf)
    return model
end

des = simulate_des(20250711)
(events_recorded = length(des.times),
 final_state = (S = des.susceptible[end], I = des.infectious[end],
                R = des.recovered[end]))
```

Note what is absent: no timestep, no loop over the population per unit time, and
no propensity calculation. The scheduler advances the clock to whichever process
is due next.

## Validation

@eq-ch08-equivalence claims this is the same process as the jump model, so an
ensemble of discrete-event runs must agree with the ODE and with the
jump-process results of @sec-jump-processes, up to Monte Carlo error.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch08-validation
grid = collect(0.0:0.5:tf)

function on_grid(model)
    values = zeros(length(grid))
    for (k, t) in enumerate(grid)
        idx = searchsortedlast(model.times, t)
        values[k] = model.infectious[max(idx, 1)]
    end
    return values
end

ensemble = [on_grid(simulate_des(21_000 + k)) for k in 1:40]
ensemble_mean = [sum(getindex.(ensemble, k))/length(ensemble) for k in eachindex(grid)]

function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    infection = β*c*u[1]*u[2]/N
    du[1] = -infection
    du[2] = infection - γ*u[2]
    du[3] = γ*u[2]
end
ode = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, [Float64(N - I₀), Float64(I₀), 0.0], (0.0, tf), nothing),
            Tsit5(); saveat = grid)

conserved = all(s + i + r == N for (s, i, r) in
                zip(des.susceptible, des.infectious, des.recovered))

(population_conserved = conserved,
 ensemble_peak = round(maximum(ensemble_mean); digits = 2),
 ode_peak = round(maximum(ode[2, :]); digits = 2),
 peak_ratio = round(maximum(ensemble_mean)/maximum(ode[2, :]); digits = 3))
```

Population is conserved exactly in every realisation, since individuals only ever
change status. The ensemble mean tracks the ODE but peaks slightly lower, for the
reason given in @sec-reaction-networks: the mean of nonlinear stochastic
trajectories is not the trajectory of the mean, and individual epidemics peak at
different times, so averaging flattens the peak.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ch08-trajectories
#| fig-cap: "Forty discrete-event realisations of the SIR process (grey), their mean (black), and the deterministic ODE (dashed). Each realisation is a different sequence of individual contacts and recoveries, so the epidemics differ in both height and timing."
figure = Figure(size = (760, 380))
axis = Axis(figure[1, 1], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Infectious")
for path in ensemble
    lines!(axis, grid, path; color = (:grey, 0.3), linewidth = 1)
end
lines!(axis, grid, ensemble_mean; color = :grey15, linewidth = 2.5,
       label = "Ensemble mean")
lines!(axis, grid, ode[2, :]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2,
       linestyle = :dash, label = "ODE")
axislegend(axis; position = :rt, framevisible = false)
figure
```

## Interpretation and limitations

Discrete-event simulation costs more bookkeeping than the jump process of
@sec-jump-processes and buys two things in return.

The first is **arbitrary waiting times**. Nothing in `life_course` requires an
exponential distribution; replacing `Exponential(1/γ)` with any other draw gives
a different infectious-period distribution immediately, with no change to the
machinery. That is the cheapest route to the non-exponential models of
@sec-non-exponential-periods, and the reason discrete-event simulation appears
before them.

The second is **contention for resources**. `ConcurrentSim` provides `Resource`
and `Store` primitives, so a model can make infectious individuals queue for a
finite number of hospital beds and record how long they wait. No compartmental
model expresses that naturally, and it is often the question a health system
actually wants answered.

The costs are real. The simulation is $O(N)$ in processes and every individual is
tracked whether or not anything is happening to them, so large populations are
expensive relative to a jump process that only tracks counts. Recording is
manual: the model above appends to vectors on every status change, which is why
the output grid must be reconstructed afterwards rather than requested. And
because each realisation is a single stochastic path, nothing can be concluded
from one run — the ensemble is the unit of analysis.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#ch08-ex1}

Replace the exponential recovery time in `life_course` with a fixed period of
$1/\gamma = 4$ time units, leaving everything else unchanged. Compare the
ensemble mean epidemic against the exponential version, and relate the direction
of the change to the generation-interval argument in
@sec-non-exponential-periods.

### Exercise 2 {#ch08-ex2}

Add a finite hospital capacity using a `ConcurrentSim` `Resource`: on becoming
infectious, an individual requests a bed, holds it for the duration of their
infectious period, and releases it on recovery. With a capacity of 50, record the
fraction of infectious individuals who fail to obtain a bed immediately and the
maximum waiting time. Explain why this quantity cannot be read off the
compartmental model of @sec-ordinary-differential-equations.
